title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
keywords: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
Public Relations Society of the Philippines
primary_topics: Chapter 12 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's keynote at the Public Relations Society of the Philippines (PRSP) Anvil Awards (February 23, 2001, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati), included in the book because it explains the Supreme Court's transparency policy and his role as centenary chair

The thesis that 'even the Supreme Court needs public relations': once 'the most inscrutable government institution' -- 'a fortress, a Mount Olympus' -- the Court must adopt transparency because it 'can be effective only insofar as it retains the long-term support of the public,' which requires being understood

The work of the Court's first-ever Committee on Public Information (chaired by CJP) and its Public Information Office (headed by Atty. Ismael G. Khan Jr.): to 'tell others the truth about the Supreme Court and its work' -- not to sanitize, angle, proselytize or propagandize -- and to give the Court a 'human face' through books on CJ Davide, a web page and simpler-language decisions

A personal and institutional frame: CJP's late father-in-law Jose A. Carpio Sr. founded the PRSP and 'elevated public relations to a profession'; the reform program's broad donor support; and a closing call for PR practitioners to help the Court disseminate the truth, since PR and judicial dispensation share 'the search for truth'
sub_topics: The Anvil Awards: CJP chaired the board of judges, which evaluated over a hundred entries; the Grand Anvil went to the Intel Philippines Science Fair as a model of 'corporate selflessness' and responsible corporate citizenship

First reason for accepting -- family: CJP's wife Leni is the daughter of the late Jose A. Carpio Sr., founding father and first president of the PRSP, first Filipino in the Public Relations Society of America, 'Dean of Filipino PR Practitioners' (first 'Gawad Panday'), who espoused corporate social consciousness and helped organize Philippine Business for Social Progress; Carpio nearly recruited CJP into his PR firm

Second reason -- the PR concepts learned from Carpio serve CJP at the Court, which two years earlier organized, 'for the first time in its 100-year history, a Committee on Public Information' that CJP chairs

The Court's former inscrutability: 'probably the most inscrutable government institution,' regarded as 'a fortress, a Mount Olympus where the gods dwelt'; the Code of Judicial Ethics limits justices' public appearances, yet they decide matters affecting everyone, and could not 'forever resist the intrusion of the Information Age'

Transparency as a worldwide trend: even the conservative US and UK supreme courts inform their publics; the Court 'can be effective only insofar as it retains the long-term support of the public,' and public acceptance of unpopular decisions requires the people's 'residual respect and esteem'

Third reason -- creating the Public Information Office and inviting Atty. Ismael G. Khan Jr. to head it; orienting justices toward transparency, simpler language and openness 'without losing the mystique and the respect due our offices'; the defining objective: 'to tell others the truth about the Supreme Court and its work,' not to 'sanitize,' 'angle,' 'proselytize' or 'propagandize'

Giving the Court a 'human face' through CJ Davide: CJP's book 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' (3,000 copies distributed), followed by 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' on the reform program, plus a Court web page; the four 'Ins' (integrity, intelligence, independence, industry) personified by Davide, named 'Filipino of the Year 2000' and rated most trusted by SWS and Pulse Asia

Pushing reform through PR: the 100th anniversary (June 11, 2001) as a 'fitting occasion' to focus on the judiciary's nation-building role and the reform agenda, which drew support from the World Bank, UNDP, USAID, Canadian CIDA, the Dutch and Belgian governments, Australian AID, ADB and the Asia Foundation

The closing call to cooperation: PR and judicial dispensation share 'the search for truth' -- the Court asks PR practitioners to help disseminate its work 'through the tested programs and tools of your profession'

An extensive photo section documenting centenary events: President Arroyo at the National Museum launch of the three-volume Centenary Reader (Aug 15, 2001); the Centennial Dinner (June 11, 2001) with foreign chief justices (Gleeson of Australia, Choudhury of Bangladesh, Xiao Yang of China, Anand of India, among others); regional celebrations (Baguio, Davao, Legaspi); the Davide closing lecture; and the Valentine's employees' program

stances.claim: 'Even the Supreme Court needs public relations.' Though its decisions are nonpolitical and 'not subject to popular vote,' the Court 'can be effective only insofar as it retains the long-term support of the public,' and public acceptance of decisions -- 'especially those that go against public opinions' -- is possible only if the institution is understood, which requires a deliberate policy of transparency. The old image of the Court as 'a fortress, a Mount Olympus' is no longer tenable in the Information Age.
stances.rhetorical_move: transparency-as-institutional-necessity: arguing that even an inherently non-majoritarian body depends on informed public esteem, so openness is a survival strategy, not a vanity
stances.confidence: asserted as the rationale for the Court's new public-information policy

stances.claim: The proper goal of the Court's public information work is simply 'to tell others the truth about the Supreme Court and its work' -- not to 'sanitize,' 'angle,' 'proselytize' or 'propagandize' -- because public relations and judicial dispensation share a basic commonality: 'the search for truth.' Transparency is truth-telling, not spin.
stances.rhetorical_move: PR-as-truth-telling: redefining public relations away from spin and aligning it with the judiciary's truth-seeking mission to legitimize the Court's outreach
stances.confidence: asserted as the defining principle of the PIO

notable_anecdotes: The PR career not taken: CJP recalls that his father-in-law Jose A. Carpio Sr. nearly convinced him, 'while still an underpaid and overworked law practitioner,' to join his PR firm as executive vice president -- but his 'Kapampangan stubbornness' made him want to stand on his own rather than rely on his kind father-in-law.

The Court as Mount Olympus: CJP describes the pre-reform Supreme Court as 'probably the most inscrutable government institution,' regarded as 'a fortress, a Mount Olympus where the gods dwelt far above and removed from the teeming crowd' -- the image transparency was meant to dispel.

Giving the Court a human face: to make the institution known, CJP wrote a book about CJ Davide ('Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard,' 3,000 copies distributed), then 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity,' and opened a Court web page -- telling interviewers in December 2000 simply to consult these about Davide before the impeachment trial.

PR judging vs the Court en banc: CJP quips that the Anvil board's three evenings of deliberation were 'comparable to those of the Supreme Court en banc' -- except there were 'more jokes and relaxing one-liners' than in the High Tribunal's 'more somber sessions.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's keynote at the PRSP Anvil Awards (February 23, 2001, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati), included in the book because it lays out the Supreme Court's transparency policy. After congratulating the Grand Anvil winner (the Intel Philippines Science Fair) as a model of corporate selflessness, CJP gives three reasons for speaking. First, family: his wife Leni is the daughter of the late Jose A. Carpio Sr., founder and first president of the PRSP and 'Dean of Filipino PR Practitioners,' who once nearly recruited CJP into his PR firm. Second, the PR concepts he learned from Carpio now serve him at the Court, which had organized 'for the first time in its 100-year history' a Committee on Public Information that he chairs. Third, he created the Public Information Office under Atty. Ismael G. Khan Jr. His governing thesis is that the once-'inscrutable' Court -- 'a fortress, a Mount Olympus' -- must embrace transparency because, though its rulings are nonpolitical, it 'can be effective only insofar as it retains the long-term support of the public,' which is possible only if the institution is understood; hence the PIO's objective is simply 'to tell others the truth about the Supreme Court and its work,' not to 'sanitize,' 'angle,' 'proselytize' or 'propagandize.' To give the Court a 'human face,' he wrote 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' (3,000 copies) and 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity,' opened a web page, and presented CJ Davide -- personifying the four 'Ins' (integrity, intelligence, independence, industry) and named 'Filipino of the Year 2000' -- as the model judge. He notes the reform program's broad support (World Bank, UNDP, USAID, CIDA, the Dutch and Belgian governments, AusAID, ADB, the Asia Foundation) and closes with a call for PR practitioners to help, since 'public relations and judicial dispensation have a basic commonality -- the search for truth.' A long photo section documents the centenary, from President Arroyo's launch of the Centenary Reader to the Centennial Dinner with visiting foreign chief justices.
